label: Surfaces Need Intersection Theory
notes: Open with the chapter's central replacement: curves carried one degree, while surfaces require pairings among divisor and curve classes. Use the six section anchors as a route map, then tell students that every later construction will be audited by the same intersection arithmetic.

label: Intersection Pairing Lattice
notes: Treat the displayed notebook artifact as the first computational dashboard. The basis H, E1, E2 makes the pairing concrete: one positive direction from the plane class and negative directions from exceptional curves. The formula on the right is the rule students should keep in their hands.

label: Self-Intersection Degree
notes: Slow down on self-intersection because it changes the meaning of degree. H behaves like the old plane degree, but exceptional curves carry negative self-intersection, and orthogonality to H records that exceptional geometry is introduced over a point. This is why surfaces are not curves with one extra coordinate.

label: Adjunction Riemann-Roch
notes: Connect adjunction and Riemann-Roch as two ways the same pairing enters global geometry. Adjunction reads genus from C squared and C dot K_X, while surface Riemann-Roch reads Euler characteristic from D dot D minus D dot K_X. The canonical class is now part of the arithmetic.

label: Hodge Index
notes: Use the cone picture to make Hodge index feel geometric rather than only spectral. The notebook check gives eigenvalues minus one, minus one, plus one in the sample basis. That means the intersection lattice has a single positive axis and many negative directions around it.

label: Nakai-Moishezon
notes: Present Nakai-Moishezon as a positivity gate, not as a vague ampleness slogan. A divisor must have positive square and positive intersection with every irreducible curve. The test explains why the earlier lattice picture matters: ampleness is detected numerically across all curve directions.

label: Ruled Coordinates
notes: Introduce ruled surfaces as the first family where two coordinates are enough for many computations. The section C0 and a fiber f have a tiny intersection table, but it already records the fibration, the base curve, and the twisting parameter e. This prepares the positivity grid.

label: Ruled Positivity Grid
notes: Read the green region in the artifact as a model ampleness computation. For D equal a C0 plus b f, the formula D squared equals two ab minus a squared e, and the normalized positivity test is a greater than zero with b greater than a e. The grid is a numerical shadow of the ruled-surface section.

label: Ruled Canonical Class
notes: Keep the canonical class formula tied to the geometry of the fibration. The coefficient of C0 records the relative projective-line direction, while the fiber coefficient remembers the genus of the base and the invariant e. The simple outputs p_g equals zero and q equals g distinguish ruled surfaces from rational surfaces.

label: Blowup Negative Class
notes: Explain a blowup as adding exactly one new negative class. Pullbacks keep the old Picard lattice, the exceptional curve contributes E squared equals minus one, and the canonical divisor shifts by E. This is the local move that later factors birational morphisms.

label: Strict Transform Accounting
notes: Use the slide-native accounting diagram to make strict transforms a readable bookkeeping rule. A curve passing through the center with multiplicity m loses m squared from self-intersection after blowup. The three bars show how multiplicity one, two, and three produce drops of one, four, and nine, which is the arithmetic signature of singular or high-multiplicity contact.

label: Embedded Resolution
notes: Use the cusp tree as an original resolution storyboard. Each blowup replaces a singular point by an exceptional direction and asks whether the strict transform still meets the exceptional locus badly. The point is the repeated accounting, not resemblance to any source diagram.

label: Cubic From Six Blowups
notes: Move from abstract blowups to the cubic surface model. Six points in the plane create six exceptional classes, and the anticanonical class three H minus the six E_i embeds the blowup as a cubic surface. The quick check K squared equals three is the numerical fingerprint.

label: Twenty-Seven Lines
notes: Organize the famous 27 lines by divisor class rather than by a spatial drawing. Six are exceptional curves, fifteen are transforms of lines through pairs of points, and six are transforms of conics through five points. The count is memorable because it comes from the same lattice.

label: Incidence Product
notes: The incidence graph is where intersection products become combinatorics. Two line classes are adjacent when their intersection product is one. The notebook check reports 27 vertices, 135 edges, and degree ten at every vertex, so the picture is backed by a finite invariant calculation.

label: Birational Factorization
notes: Frame birational morphisms as chains of monoidal moves. Instead of trying to draw a rational map directly, resolve its indeterminacy upstairs, then compare the two downward morphisms. This common-resolution picture explains why blowups and contractions are the grammar of surface birational geometry.

label: Castelnuovo Minimality
notes: Castelnuovo's criterion runs the blowup arithmetic backward. A rational curve with self-intersection minus one can be contracted to a nonsingular point, removing one negative exceptional direction. Minimality means no such contractible exceptional curve remains on the model being studied.

label: Classification Geography
notes: Treat the classification chart as schematic geography, just as the notebook does. Kodaira dimension separates rational and ruled surfaces, zero-canonical families, elliptic surfaces, and general type. The linked lab is useful because it keeps the birational markers visible without pretending to replace classification theory.

label: Recap Arithmetic Engine
notes: Close by returning to the one arithmetic engine. The lattice, ruled grid, blowup update, and cubic incidence graph look different, but all are inspections of intersection numbers plus checks. The computational audit trail gives students confidence that the visuals are teaching invariants rather than ornament.
